newsitem.title: UK: French franc wobbled by appetite for rainy day options.
newsitem.headline: French franc wobbled by appetite for rainy day options.

text.p: The sudden and unexpected hiccup in the French franc against the mark this week at least partly reflects rising investor interest in cheap insurance against one last currency blowout before European monetary union.

That cheap insurance is most obvious in the options market, where buying the right to purchase marks, or mark calls, against the franc over the next six-to-12 months, for example, has been seen by many players this week, some as good value padding against the risk that the home run to EMU in 1999 trips up.

Because options are priced as a function of the historical and implied volatility of an exchange rate, the recent stability of the mark/French franc exchange rate and optimism about a punctual start for EMU meant the price of these options have skidded to bargain-bin levels that were difficult to ignore.

"What is clear is that mark/Paris implied volatilty is so low that some players have been happy to pick up mark calls and leave them in the bottom drawer -- just in case," said Teis Knuthsen, economist at First Chicago in London.

The rumblings of discontent in Paris this week about the government's 10-year old policy of franc fort, or strong franc, have highlighted enough risks to longer-term mark/franc stability to prompt investors to at least cover their backs, traders said.
A can of worms was opened by former French president Valery Giscard d'Estaing on Tuesday when he called for a depreciation of the franc across the borad to the equivalent of 3.65 per mark.
The franc weakened today to a two-month low against the mark at 3.3975 but recovered some ground a little later in the European session to 3.3890.

Giscard's comment attracted public support from more typical EMU-sceptic French politicians like Pierre Mazeaud, Phillipe Seguin and Charles Pasqua, despite official dismissals of the idea from the unpopular Prime Minister Alain Juppe.

Market jitters about the comments were heightened because of persistent rumours of an early-1997 cabinet reshuffle which some analysts believed may take on more influence from the Seguin/Pasqua wing of the ruling RPR party.

The sustained parity between 10-year French and German bond yields, for example, shows longer-term capital flows have not yet been disturbed by the latest jitters and most believe EMU will start with France in 1999.
But, analysts said there is appetite to protect against any last-minute stage fright in the final countdown next year to irrevocable exchange rate fixing.
The bottom line is that it costs very little to do so.

Implied volatility in one-year mark/franc options had fallen to as low as 1.70 percent over the past two months, with implied volatility down to 1.40 percent for one-month options. This compares with an implied one-year volatility, for example, of 7.70 percent for dollar/mark options.

However, the slide in the franc's spot rate this week and the rise in options demand has seen one-year implied volatility in mark/franc jump to 2.50 percent today. One-month popped over 3.0 percent at one point late Thursday, traders said.

"Nearly all French franc markets have been so tightly priced in recent months that there has got to be value in betting against them unless you believe there is an absolute 110 percent certainty of EMU starting on time," said Paul Meggyesi, senior currency strategist at Deutsche Morghan Grenfell.

Traders cited brisk demand for out-of-the-money options to buy marks - options with exercise prices far from the current spot rates. One major U.S. investment firm and one of the big three Swiss banks was particularly active, traders said.
"The 3.70 strike has traded a lot lately, with these things trading for peanuts," said one trader at a U.S. investment firm.
One-year options with exercise prices, or strikes, as high as 3.70 francs per mark were cited by many traders, with one saying total trades this week exceeded one billion marks.
"There has been good two-way trade in one-year mark/Paris options with strikes at 3.70 which helped the bullish tone of the mark," said Andrew Chaveriat, analyst at Banque Paribas.
